Where it began

Mohammad Azharuddin was born in Hyderabad on 8 February 1963. Cricket came to him through the family: an uncle on his mother's side had led the Osmania University team, and the young Azhar wanted to follow. A teacher at All Saints High School, Brother K. M. Joseph, fed the habit too.

He started out bowling seam, then moved up to bat at number three for Hyderabad Schools. At 18 he played his first Ranji Trophy match for Hyderabad, in the 1981–82 season, and the runs soon poured in: 2,648 of them in 1982–83 alone. A double hundred in the Duleep Trophy and a hundred in each innings against Andhra made the selectors look his way.

The player

He came into the side against England at Eden Gardens on the last day of 1984 and made 110. Then he made hundreds in the next two Tests as well. Nobody before him had begun a Test career with three in three.

In 99 Tests from 1984 to 2000 he scored 6,215 runs at 45.04, with 22 hundreds and 21 fifties, and his best was 199 against Sri Lanka at Kanpur in 1986, when he and Kapil Dev put on 272 together. He also held 105 catches. He was made captain in 1989 and led India in 47 Tests, winning 14 of them, a record for an Indian captain at the time. In one-day cricket he lifted the Asia Cup twice and took India to the semi-finals of the 1996 World Cup.

What made him special

It was all in the wrists. Srinivasaraghavan Venkataraghavan thought nobody in the game had better ones, and he batted with an ease that made hard things look simple. England saw the best of it in 1990: 121 at Lord's, described by Vic Marks as the most dazzling Test hundred he had seen, then 179 at Old Trafford, and 426 runs in the series at 85.20.

Against South Africa in 1996–97 he reached a hundred at Kolkata off just 74 balls, equal with Kapil Dev as the fastest by an Indian, and followed it with an unbeaten 163 as India won by 280 runs. His bowling never troubled the scorers' wicket column, but with a bat like his, it hardly needed to.

Away from the middle

India gave him the Arjuna Award in 1986 and the Padma Shri in 1988, and Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1991. In 2019 he was elected president of the Hyderabad Cricket Association, back in the city where it all started. He also went into public life and was elected to parliament in 2009. In 2023 Jamia Hamdard in New Delhi gave him an honorary doctorate.

And finally

His last Test, against South Africa at Bangalore in March 2000, brought a hundred, 102 of them. That made him the first Indian, and only the fifth batsman anywhere, to make a hundred in both his first Test and his last. Few careers have such tidy bookends.
